title: Spindle-Hour Options: Reserve Capacity, Skip Inventory
one_liner: Standardized capacity-reservation contracts that let OEMs hedge supply risk by paying a small premium for guaranteed machining hours.
customer: Procurement leads at $50M-$1B OEMs (industrial equipment, medical devices, defense subcontractors) and 10-100 person job shops with idle spindles.
problem: 57% of negative ISM comments cite price volatility, and one respondent called lead times worse than the pandemic era. Machine-shop owners report buying a full year of inventory to lock in prices. That ties up cash and risks obsolescence. Marketplaces sell only spot capacity, and shops cannot get predictable base load.
solution: A standard reservation contract by machine class (3-axis, 5-axis, Swiss, wire EDM, weld cell). The buyer pays a reservation fee for N hours a month over 6-12 months at a strike rate, with materials indexed to published metals prices. The buyer exercises by releasing drawings within 10 days. The platform vets shops, holds deposits in escrow, and resells unexercised hours to spot buyers.
why_now: Metals repricing under Section 232, Hormuz freight shocks, machinery hiring picking up, and auto-supplier capacity going idle. Buyers can no longer count on spot capacity appearing.
revenue_model: 6-10% of reservation fees plus 2-3% of exercised work. Later, underwrite a portfolio of options for the spread.
non_obvious_insight: A job shop's most valuable asset is certainty of base load, and it will discount 10-20% for take-or-pay. Buyers fear not getting parts more than they fear price. An option on capacity is a cheaper hedge than a year of inventory, and the deposit doubles as working capital for the shop.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 shops with one machine class in one region (for example Northeast Ohio). Draft a two-page contract with a manufacturing lawyer. Pitch 15 buyers who are already stockpiling inventory. Aim for $50k in reservations by day 60. Run it as a brokerage first.

title: Screwworm-Era Rescue Transport Compliance Desk
one_liner: With screwworm confirmed in Texas, dogs leaving Texas and New Mexico need a fresh vet inspection certificate and destination permits; run the compliance desk that keeps shelter transports moving.
customer: Texas and New Mexico shelters, rescue transport organizations (ground and air), destination shelters in other states, and the funders who pay for transport.
problem: New World screwworm was first confirmed in Texas on 2026-06-03, with movement restrictions in infested zones across a growing list of counties. Reports say dogs from Texas and New Mexico now need a certificate of veterinary inspection within 72 hours of movement that attests no wounds infested with screwworm. Receiving states add entry permits and pre-travel inspections five to seven days out, shelter transports are slowing, and accredited vets are scarce for 20-100 animal loads.
solution: A transport desk with a destination-state rules engine, permit and eCVI orchestration, scheduling of mobile inspection crews (floating DVM plus techs) at pickup sites, a treatment log for authorized products, manifests, and rejection-risk alerts before a truck leaves.
why_now: Screwworm's first US detection (June 2026), FDA emergency authorizations for animal drugs (15 EUAs and 3 conditional approvals as of 2026-09-03), and state zone orders have changed movement rules mid-season. Shelters are crowded and funders are looking for what unblocks flow.
revenue_model: $15-35 per animal moved, mobile inspection crew fees, and SaaS for destination shelters. Costs often covered by transport grants.
non_obvious_insight: Rescue transport is treated as a charity logistics problem. The new binding constraints are regulatory paperwork and scarce accredited-vet hours, which is a compliance-ops business with per-animal pricing. The same rails will be reused for the next outbreak (H5N1, canine influenza, rabies rule changes).
first_30_days: Call 10 Texas shelters and transport groups. Put the top 5 destination-state rule sets into a spreadsheet. Run 2 transports with hired mobile-vet pickup inspections at $20 per animal. Approach transport-grant funders for direct payment.

title: Model-Swap Regression Service for Contractors
one_liner: Automated testing and porting that lets defense contractors re-platform their AI workflows to a different model vendor in weeks without losing quality.
customer: Defense integrators, primes' AI teams and mid-size government contractors whose workflows were tuned around one model family and must now change vendors.
problem: The D.C. Circuit upheld the DoD supply-chain-risk designation of one model vendor on Sept 26, and DoD is moving classified workloads off it by October. Contractors are cutting that vendor's use. Their prompts, agents and evaluation sets were tuned for one model, and nobody can prove a replacement performs equally on their real tasks.
solution: Capture the contractor's existing workflow traces, build a task-specific eval set, run it across Gemini, ChatGPT, Grok and open-weight models, and auto-rewrite prompts and tool schemas to reach parity. Deliver a signed parity report usable as evidence for the government customer.
why_now: The designation is a fresh legal fact with an October deadline. Vendor politics now shape the supply chain, and lawful-use terms differ by vendor. Model swapping is now a compliance event, not an engineering preference.
revenue_model: $40-200K per migration project, then $3-10K per month for continuous cross-vendor regression monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: The designation is not a one-time event. Every future vendor dispute will force the same migration, so the durable product is a standing eval-and-port harness for a politically volatile model market.
first_30_days: Post a fixed-price migration audit at $15K. Contact 15 small integrators and GenAI.mil agent builders through defense AI communities. Reuse one eval harness across clients while keeping each client's data separate.

title: Crop Scouts of the Sea for Seafood Buyers
one_liner: A paid panel of working skippers and tender operators that texts in daily run, quality and delivery-limit data, sold to seafood buyers and lenders days to weeks before the market sees it.
customer: Wild-salmon importers and distributors, club-store and retail category buyers, Japanese and European trading houses, canned and frozen sockeye brokers, banks lending to processors, reinsurers and commodity funds. Each pays $10-30K/year. Panelists are paid, so fishermen are also customers of the cash flow.
problem: Bristol Bay is the source of most of the world's wild sockeye, and price went from $1.03/lb avg in 2025 (41.2M fish) to $1.72/lb in 2026 (30.1M fish). Farmed Atlantic salmon has futures and analyst coverage. Wild sockeye has neither. Buyers see ADF&G escapement and harvest counts and press releases, but not fish size, color, quality, roe, which processors are on delivery limits, tender backlogs, or which plants are paying up for fish. That information reaches the market 2-4 weeks late, after forward prices are already set.
solution: Recruit 150-300 skippers, crew and tender operators. Each sends a 60-second daily check-in (pounds per boat, average fish weight, limit status by processor, hours waiting at the tender, water temp, color and quality, weather, gear). Validate it against ADF&G counts and AIS. Publish a daily 'Fisher's Report' with the run-timing curve, quality and limit maps, and proprietary indexes, plus a weekly call with a retired skipper as analyst. Extend to Copper River, Prince William Sound, Kodiak and Southeast.
why_now: The one-year 67% swing in average price has made buyers and lenders hungry for earlier signals. Alt-data buyers already pay for crop scouts and satellite counts in other commodities. Starlink on boats makes real-time reporting possible. LLMs can clean messy text reports into structured data at almost no cost.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $12-30K/year per company, custom data feeds at $50K+, and analyst calls. Pay panelists $150-400 per season out of 20-30% of revenue. Add other fisheries and other 'boots on the ground' sectors later.
non_obvious_insight: Information in the fleet moves at VHF speed. The whole fleet knows the run is late, the fish are small, or the tenders are backed up days before any official number, and buyers treat it as noise. Skippers will happily share anonymized volume and quality data if you pay them, because it does not touch their contract terms or fishing spots. The valuable part is aggregation and a track record. Keep panelists' data separate from any confidential processor contract terms, and get securities and antitrust counsel before selling to funds.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 panelists from Facebook groups and associations while everyone is idle after settlements. Ask them for 2026 season logs (many keep daily notes and fish tickets). Backtest against ADF&G data and the 2026 price path, and show the panel's signals would have led the market. Send a sample '2026 in hindsight' report to 30 importers and analysts. Aim for 3 pilot subscriptions at about $5K each before the May opener.

title: PFAS-Cleared Succession for Plating Shops
one_liner: Fixed-price wastewater and PFAS readiness reports that let retiring plating and anodizing owners sell to buyers and lenders, feeding a buyer marketplace.
customer: Retiring owners of metal-finishing shops, industrial business brokers, SBA lenders and search-fund or roll-up buyers, at $9-18k per report plus a success fee.
problem: About 60% of manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+, and reshoring and defense customers cannot find finishing capacity (plating, anodizing, passivation). Wet-process shops carry discharge permits, sludge records and historic PFAS exposure that stall buyers' and lenders' diligence, so shops close instead of transferring.
solution: A standardized wet-shop report covering permit and sewer-use history, a PFAS use inventory and sampling, sludge manifests and quoted closed-loop upgrades. Add a clean-up and certification package, then match certified shops to buyers.
why_now: Reshoring is happening inside existing buildings. POTWs are hunting PFAS sources ahead of 2027 monitoring. Compass-type roll-ups are buying shops, and the MMS admits no dataset of owners near retirement exists.
revenue_model: Report fee, 1% success fee on transactions, and remediation referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real reshoring bottleneck is finishing, not machining. Finishing shops cannot change hands because water liabilities are unpriced, so whoever prices them owns the deal flow.
first_30_days: Call 10 industrial business brokers and the metal-finishing trade association. Do two discounted reports. Publish a one-page checklist to build a lead list of owners.

title: Verified-Guardian Credential Built on Childcare Centers
one_liner: Start as a custody-aware pickup and consent app for childcare centers, then turn those institutions into issuers of privacy-preserving 'verified parent of a child aged X' tokens that apps pay for.
customer: First: childcare centers, camps and youth orgs (SaaS at $50-150 per site per month). Later: app stores, game studios and platforms (per-attestation fees), and state agencies.
problem: Parental-consent laws (Ohio, Florida, Texas and others) need a verified parent, but credit-card or ID checks prove adulthood, not parenthood. OS vendors will supply age attestation but not guardian relationships. Meanwhile childcare centers and schools already verify guardian-child relationships, custody orders and authorized pickup, and that verification is not reusable.
solution: Phase 1 is a check-in and pickup app with ID and liveness verification for guardians, custody-order parsing, an authorized pickup list, and e-consent for photos, trips and immunizations. Phase 2 lets the center vouch, through zero-knowledge or selective-disclosure tokens, that an adult is a verified guardian of a child in an age band, without revealing identities to apps.
why_now: Consent laws took effect in mid-2026, OS-level age signals exist (California, Texas), and age-verification breaches have made 'verify once, store nothing' attractive. Zero-knowledge age-proof libraries appeared in 2025 (from memory), and the brief identifies guardian and consent workflows as the gap OS vendors won't fill.
revenue_model: Center SaaS ($50-150 per site per month) now, and per-attestation fees ($0.10-0.50) from platforms later, with revenue share to issuing centers.
non_obvious_insight: Identity startups verify people, but the missing primitive is verifying a relationship. The institutions that already do it (childcare centers with custody paperwork) form an unmonetized, fragmented long tail.
first_30_days: Interview 20 center directors about pickup disputes and custody paperwork. Build an MVP with QR pickup and a custody-document vault. Sell 10 centers at $79 a month. Integrate an ID-verification vendor for guardian checks and sketch the token format with a privacy engineer.

title: FEOC and Cyber Passport for Batteries
one_liner: A serial-number-level ledger of material-assistance content and firmware and comms attestations for storage projects, built for tax-credit buyers and insurers.
customer: C&I and utility-scale storage developers and integrators, tax-credit transfer buyers (banks and insurers), and lenders.
problem: FEOC rules require 55% non-FEOC content for storage starting construction in 2026, rising to 75% by 2030. About 80% of US cells are Chinese and non-compliant projects run about 43% pricier. IRS cost tables are not due until 2027, so nobody can prove compliance. Buyers of tax credits and insurers need evidence, and concern about undocumented radios in imported inverters adds a cyber layer.
solution: A workflow and ledger that captures the bill of materials at cell and module level with supplier attestations and cost tables, then computes the material-assistance ratio conservatively. Each project gets an audit-ready evidence packet. Optional teardown, RF and firmware attestation runs through a partner lab. The 'passport' is what transfer buyers and insurers accept.
why_now: FEOC applies to 2026 construction starts, the tax-credit transfer market is doing diligence at scale, and tariffs are rising.
revenue_model: $15-50k per project, $2-5k a month SaaS per developer, verification fees from transfer buyers, and cost-plus lab attestation.
non_obvious_insight: The burden is evidence, not sourcing. With IRS guidance missing, the first firm whose conservative methodology gets accepted becomes the de facto standard, and insurers will only underwrite recapture cover against that record.
first_30_days: Publish a free MACR calculator with conservative assumptions. Interview 10 developers and three tax-credit transfer buyers. Sell three paid compliance-file builds at ~$15k for 2026-start projects. Pre-agree terms with an attestation lab.

title: Step-Up Basis Files for Inherited Assets
one_liner: Sell CPAs and estate lawyers a cheap, defensible date-of-death valuation packet for every inherited house or portfolio.
customer: CPAs and enrolled agents preparing 1040s and 1041s for heirs, estate attorneys, and heirs selling inherited homes or securities.
problem: The step-up in basis (IRC 1014) is the biggest tax break most families receive, but only if the heir can support date-of-death value. Below the estate-tax threshold no appraisal is required, so heirs sell years later with no valuation and risk the IRS asserting the parent's low original cost. Securities and crypto also need clean date-of-death pricing.
solution: A $150-$400 per-asset packet: houses (AVM plus retrospective appraiser sign-off), securities (date-of-death pricing), crypto, collectibles. It outputs a Basis Memo for the CPA's file, stores it, and alerts the heir when the property lists for sale.
why_now: The higher federal exemption (reported $15M) means fewer estates file a Form 706 that would have documented values. Home prices are sharply higher than a few years ago, so embedded gains are large. Boomers are the source of most transfers.
revenue_model: Per-report fees, CPA firm subscriptions, and appraiser marketplace margin.
non_obvious_insight: The tax benefit is lost through missing paperwork, not law. A small, cheap document created at death protects a large tax saving years later.
first_30_days: Sell to 15 CPA firms and 5 estate attorneys. Use an AVM API plus 3 contract appraisers per metro. Deliver in 5 business days and gather feedback on what the CPAs actually attach to returns.

title: Certified Refurb Phone Pipeline for Africa
one_liner: The memory crunch kills the cheap new phone, so the next wave of African users arrives on graded, warrantied used handsets.
customer: Independent phone retailers and mid-size distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana, and telco handset-financing programmes.
problem: Memory is 30-40% of a phone's bill of materials, IDC calls sub-Rs 9,000 phones possibly permanently uneconomical, and the GSMA $40 phone is only a pilot. About 960M Africans under coverage are still offline, and the used-phone market is full of blacklisted, dying-battery lemons.
solution: Buy bulk trade-in lots from the Gulf, EU and Japan and grade them in software (battery health, IMEI/blacklist check, Play certification). Ship with a 6-month warranty and sell to retailers on 30-day credit. The wedge is IMEI-clean, warrantied lots for a handful of retailers in one market such as Lagos.
why_now: 2026 AI-driven memory prices broke the sub-$60 new-phone tier, and LatAm shipments fell 10%. The GSMA is piloting a $40 phone precisely because the market cannot produce one.
revenue_model: Roughly $8-15 gross margin per handset, plus warranty fees and a financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for cheap new phones. The scarce asset is trust in used devices, and whoever certifies them owns the affordable tier once new supply disappears.
first_30_days: Source about 500 units from a Dubai or European refurbisher, grade them and place them with five retailers on consignment. Track return rates, which become the pricing moat.

title: Heat and Smoke Stop-Day Kit for Outdoor Crews
one_liner: Text-message heat and smoke compliance for small outdoor employers, sold through comp carriers and PEOs, with parametric stop-day cover to follow.
customer: Workers' comp carriers and PEOs serving small landscapers, roofers, framers and farms in California, Washington and Oregon (later AZ, TX, CO), plus general contractors that need subs' plans.
problem: OSHA's federal heat rule has slipped (supplemental proposal Dec 2026, final Oct 2027), but California, Washington and Oregon already bind employers. Small crews have no written plan, acclimatization tracking or go/no-go rule. Heat and smoke stop-work days hurt small-contractor cash flow, and business-interruption cover for them is barely productized.
solution: Phase one is a text-message-first kit: site-level heat and air-quality alerts, a state-specific written plan, water, shade and break logs, acclimatization schedules and audit exports. Phase two adds parametric stop-day cover through an MGA partner, with WBGT or AQI triggers.
why_now: The summer 2026 shock and state rules make compliance urgent, while federal delay pushes pressure onto carriers and GCs.
revenue_model: $39-99 per crew per month, or per-employee fees from carriers and PEOs for loss control, plus parametric premium margin later.
non_obvious_insight: Demand does not depend on OSHA. States, general-contractor prequalification and comp-carrier loss control drive it.
first_30_days: Pitch two comp-carrier loss-control teams and a landscaping association. Run a 20-crew pilot with the plan generator and alerts.

title: Parametric Cover Against Career-Field Collapse
one_liner: Index-based protection that pays out when hiring in a specific occupation falls past a threshold, sold first to bootcamps, income-share funds and private student lenders whose job-guarantee promises are now correlated bets on entry-level demand.
customer: Bootcamps with job guarantees, ISA funds, private student lenders and university tuition-protection programs. Later, workers via employers and universities as a benefit.
problem: These institutions underwrite outcomes assuming stable entry-level demand. If CS, marketing or analytics hiring drops 30% they all fail together, and no hedge exists. The tail risk is now visible (22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend, junior tech postings down ~35% in major EU countries in 2024).
solution: Phase 1 (about 6 months): publish an Occupation Demand Index (postings, hires, claims mix by occupation and metro) plus stress-test analytics, sold as a subscription to lenders and ISA funds. Phase 2: structure parametric covers through an MGA, fronting carrier and reinsurers, triggered by the index. Phase 3: consumer livelihood cover via employers and universities.
why_now: Occupation-level posting data (e.g. Indeed Hiring Lab) is rich, AI exposure is a new correlated risk, parametric insurance infrastructure has matured, ISA funds and bootcamps are under strain, and event-contract markets are normalised.
revenue_model: Analytics subscriptions ($30-120k a year) first, then premiums and ceding commissions.
non_obvious_insight: Occupational risk has never been hedged because individual triggers create moral hazard. An index solves that for institutions whose portfolio effectively is the occupation, and AI displacement is exactly the correlated tail that reinsurers price.
first_30_days: Build the index from public BLS and posting data and backtest against bootcamp outcome reports. Pitch 10 ISA funds, bootcamps and private lenders a paid $10-25k stress-test pilot.

title: O-1 Evidence Vault as a Startup Employee Benefit
one_liner: Continuously captures, verifies and time-stamps the evidence that O-1A, EB-1A and NIW petitions are actually won on, so a lawyer can file in weeks instead of scrambling for six months.
customer: Venture-backed startups and AI labs with foreign-born staff pay $25-40 per employee per month. Founders, PhD students and researchers can use a self-serve tier. Immigration firms license a white-label version.
problem: The $100k fee on new H-1B petitions for workers abroad, and a wage-weighted lottery for everyone else, have pushed tech employers toward O-1A, EB-1A and NIW as the primary route. But these are evidence-driven cases. Clients show up with nothing organized, the lawyer spends weeks chasing citation counts, salary comparisons, press links and reference letters, letters end up as boilerplate, and half the evidence (paid associations, vanity press, generic membership) gets discounted by adjudicators at the final-merits stage anyway. AI-generated petitions are now a recognizable genre officers discount.
solution: A vault that connects to sources people already have (OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar, Google Scholar, GitHub/Hugging Face adoption, patents, OpenReview and conference reviewer rosters, Wayback-archived press, compensation data with consent) and adds structured quarterly manager memos documenting the employee's critical role. It logs each independent-expert letter request with dates and independence facts. Output is a criterion-by-criterion evidence map with gaps and a plain-language six-month plan, plus a flag for evidence types officers typically discount. It hands the packet to any immigration lawyer, including the employer's existing counsel.
why_now: The H-1B fee and lottery weighting since late 2025 have made O-1A and EB-1A a mainstream path rather than an exception for founders and stars. AI labs and startups need it for dozens of employees at once, so time-to-file matters. Public scholarly and code metadata are now available through open APIs, and LLMs make it feasible to structure messy evidence at low cost.
revenue_model: Per-employee SaaS ($25-40 per month), a $300-500 one-time evidence audit, and a licensing fee from law firms. Immigration counsel remains separate, and no fee-splitting occurs.
non_obvious_insight: Petitions are decided on what was already documented by the time the client met the lawyer. Nobody builds evidence continuously because no one owns the job: HR doesn't know the criteria, lawyers only engage after the decision to file, and employees don't know what counts. Separately, the evidence that counts (independent judging, real citations, critical-role documentation) is often free to collect early and impossible to fabricate later, while the paid pay-to-play tactics sold to nervous applicants are actively harmful.
first_30_days: Find 3 seed or Series A AI startups with heavily foreign-born teams, through their immigration counsel or investor platform teams. Run a manual concierge audit for 20 employees at $300 each, producing the criterion-by-criterion map in a spreadsheet plus Google Doc. Identify the top 5 recurring evidence gaps (they will be the same across companies) and automate those first. Convert the startups to a subscription once the first two employees file petitions faster than expected.

title: Pre-Permitted School Suites for Micro-Schools
one_liner: Master-lease vacant office and retail suites, pre-solve the change-of-use to educational occupancy, and rent furnished seats by the student to micro-school operators funded by education savings accounts.
customer: Micro-school networks and guides (per-student monthly seat rent), landlords of vacant suites (a paying tenant with no build-out risk), and ESA-funded parents underneath.
problem: Universal ESAs are minting demand: Texas alone funds $10,474 per student for 2026-27, drew 130,000+ applications in the first three weeks, and micro-school networks like Primer are opening campuses to serve it. The gate is the certificate of occupancy, not curriculum or demand. More than five children generally triggers Group E in the building code, and founders discover egress, restroom count, fire alarm and ADA gaps after signing a lease. Landlords have no standard lease and fear liability. AI-guided micro-schools need only about 25-40 sq ft per student and a few hours of adaptive software.
solution: A master-lessee that holds a portfolio of pre-engineered suites (ground floor, existing restrooms, former daycare, church, tutoring or medical use) with permit packages per jurisdiction. It subleases furnished seats month to month with a cancellation clause if ESA funding lapses, standard landlord-friendly leases and pooled insurance, plus an opening checklist and inspector relationships.
why_now: Texas ESAs go live in 2026-27 and the federal tax-credit scholarship program begins in 2027, on top of a dozen-plus states with existing ESAs. Office vacancy is 17.8%, maturity-wall landlords will take any creditworthy tenant, and the school-age population is shifting toward small-cohort, phone-light models.
revenue_model: Spread between master lease and per-seat rent (25-35% gross margin), TI financing fees, and a subscription for operators to use the permit-pack library.
non_obvious_insight: Micro-school growth is gated by a building department, not by families or teachers. The party that holds the permits, not the curriculum, owns the supply chain, and vacant offices are the wrong space until someone pre-solves the change of use.
first_30_days: Pick Texas (Austin, Dallas, Houston or San Antonio) and map 40 vacant suites with existing daycare or ground-floor restroom stock. Sign one or two 12-month master leases. Pre-sell three operators and open one site by January 2027 for spring enrollment. Get a code consultant to write a reusable permit checklist.

title: Church-Basement Microschools for Retired Teachers
one_liner: A turnkey venue, insurance, fire-code and ESA-billing kit that lets a retired teacher open an 8-15 student paid school in a congregation's empty weekday classrooms.
customer: Retired or soon-to-retire teachers aged 55-70 pay a monthly fee and a share of tuition. Congregations are the landlords. Parents are the end payers, through education savings account (ESA) funds.
problem: Microschool builders assume curriculum and tech are the hard part. What actually kills these schools is the certificate of occupancy and zoning, the fire marshal, liability insurance, ESA vendor approval and reimbursement paperwork, and bookkeeping. Retired teachers have the credibility and skills but no business experience. Meanwhile congregations hold Sunday-school classrooms that sit empty Monday to Friday and need rent.
solution: A state-by-state permit packet (occupancy class, what the inspector will actually ask for). A pre-negotiated group liability policy for microschools. A standard five-day lease with congregations covering rent, cleaning, security and safeguarding. Onboarding for ESA and voucher programs (including any accreditation or approved-provider requirements) plus back-office billing and attendance. A menu of curricula so the teacher chooses. A shared bench of substitute retired teachers for sick days.
why_now: Texas launched its Education Freedom Accounts in fall 2026 with $1 billion, about $10,474 per student in 2026-27 (a 12-student school is roughly $125k in revenue), and about 600 private schools and pre-K providers applied in the first 10 days. Universal or near-universal ESAs are live in a growing list of states, and a federal scholarship tax credit begins in 2027. About 1.5 million students are already in microschools, and teacher retirements are climbing.
revenue_model: $199-$399/month platform fee per school, about 4% of tuition processed, insurance commissions, and a 5% lease-admin fee from congregations.
non_obvious_insight: Pension re-employment caps generally bite when you return to a covered public district. Working for yourself in a private school usually does not touch your annuity (verify by state), and past full retirement age the Social Security earnings test no longer applies. So a retired teacher can keep her pension and collect full tuition. Parents' top trust signal is 'Mrs. Alvarez taught 31 years at Lincoln Elementary.' A church building that is already zoned, already inspected for children, and rents for $800-$1,500 a month is the cost moat. Curriculum is commodity. Occupancy and insurance are the moat.
first_30_days: In Texas or Arizona or Florida, recruit a cohort of 10 retired teachers through retired-educator associations and Facebook groups. Line up 5 congregations with weekday space. Build the permit checklist for one city, get one group insurance quote, and sign 3 pilot schools at $299/month. Target the January 2027 semester and the early-2027 ESA application cycle for 2027-28, since fall 2026 enrollment has already closed.

title: Do-Not-Transact Registry: GAMSTOP for Scams
one_liner: An opt-in registry, controlled by consumers and their families, that crypto ATMs, gift-card sellers and wire desks must check before completing a high-risk transaction.
customer: Crypto-ATM operators and gift-card retailers (paying per check and for legal cover). People enroll for free through credit unions, senior centers and adult children.
problem: Crypto-ATM fraud losses rose 58% to $389M in 2025, 66% of it from victims aged 60+. Older adults lost $7.7B overall. Education campaigns fail because scammers coach victims mid-scam to bypass warnings. State AGs have sued major kiosk operators, and cities are considering bans.
solution: People (or a family member with their consent) register commitments made while calm: no cash-to-crypto, no gift cards above $X, no new-payee wires above $Y, bound to ID number and phone. Kiosks that already scan IDs, and retailers via API at gift-card purchase, check the registry and show a neutral refusal script. Lifting a block takes a 72-hour cooling-off period, which breaks the scammer's urgency.
why_now: State kiosk laws (daily caps, mandatory warnings, refunds) and AG lawsuits give operators an urgent need to prove diligence. IC3's 2025 data quantified the elder-loss concentration. Operators may soon need a defensible control to keep their licenses.
revenue_model: About $0.05-0.25 per check plus $500-2K per month per operator. Gift-card processors and retail chains by contract. Grants and credit-union sponsorships fund enrollment.
non_obvious_insight: UK self-exclusion for gambling works because people commit in a calm moment. Scam prevention has assumed you can persuade people mid-scam, which fails. A registry turns consumer protection into a B2B compliance lookup that operators buy for legal cover, so the payer is not the person at risk.
first_30_days: Build an enrollment page and a kiosk-check API. Pilot with one independent operator (100-500 kiosks) and one state credit-union league, and enroll the first 1,000 people through a credit union or senior center. Use the results to brief state legislators and the AG's office.

title: Blind Spend Tokens for Secretive Buyer Agents
one_liner: A buyer-side privacy gateway that lets agents pay for data and APIs with unlinkable tokens that prove 'authorized and funded' without revealing who is asking, what the price ceiling is, or what the question was.
customer: Buy-side and R&D organizations whose queries are the secret: hedge funds and asset managers, pharma competitive-intelligence and BD teams, M&A law firms and defense contractors that route agents to paid data, patent, expert-network and search APIs.
problem: Agent commerce protocols hand the seller the buyer's leverage by design. Signed mandates state a maximum price and intent, agent IDs let vendors profile and price-discriminate, and the queries themselves (a ticker, a compound, a patent family) reveal research direction. Query logs can leak, be resold or be front-run.
solution: A gateway sitting between the buyer's agents and vendors. Blind-signed, unlinkable spend tokens (Privacy Pass style) are issued after KYC by a bank or escrow, so the vendor is guaranteed payment but cannot identify the buyer. Mandates are committed and proven within cap using a zero-knowledge range proof or a TEE mediator, so the ceiling is never disclosed. Queries are batched, cached and mixed with decoys across a pooled anonymity set of customers.
why_now: Signed-agent identity and KYA schemes are proliferating across card networks and web standards, all oriented toward reassuring sellers. Privacy Pass is now a set of IETF standards. Agents issue thousands of paid queries per day, so leakage volume has exploded.
revenue_model: $8-25k per month per firm plus 0.5-1% of pass-through spend. A one-time $15k query-leakage audit is the entry product.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is building 'know your agent' for the seller's benefit. The buyer's reservation price and research intent are the real assets, and privacy for the buyer is unclaimed territory. For funds, leaked query patterns are alpha decay, which gives a hard-dollar budget line. The chicken-and-egg problem of anonymity sets is solved by starting with decoy traffic and TEE-operated pooling.
first_30_days: Sell 5 query-leakage audits ($15k each) to funds and pharma CI teams: instrument what their agents leak to vendors (headers, mandates, IPs, query text) and deliver a report. Turn the audit findings into a decoy-plus-proxy gateway for the three data vendors most used by early customers.

title: Retiring Masters' Exit Interviews, Funded by Employers and AI Labs
one_liner: Capture the last generation of unrecorded tradespeople as expert playbooks for their employer and consented, royalty-bearing training data for robotics and industrial-AI labs.
customer: Two payers. Operations and HR leaders at municipal water and wastewater utilities, electric co-ops, machine shops and food plants pay $6-15k per retiring expert. Robotics and maintenance-copilot companies pay to license consented expert demonstration data.
problem: Decades of tacit knowledge walk out the door with baby-boomer retirees: why a pump sounds wrong, how to set up a difficult mold, what to check third when the obvious fixes fail. Written SOPs miss it. Robotics labs can buy cheap novice chore video but have almost no expert-grade manipulation and diagnostic-reasoning data, and crowd-sourced gig filming is hitting a quality ceiling.
solution: A two-person crew, or a mailed camera kit plus a remote interviewer, spends 2-3 days per expert: head-mounted and wrist cameras during real tasks, think-aloud narration, 'what would you check next?' probing, and staged edge cases. Deliverables: (1) an employer-owned playbook of video-indexed SOPs, fault libraries and decision trees, plus a searchable Q&A bot; (2) a de-identified dataset licensed to AI and robotics buyers. The expert gets a retention bonus and a royalty share, and the employer gets a discount in exchange for licensing rights.
why_now: The physical-AI and humanoid boom created a 2025-26 scramble for demonstration data, and large labs and gig apps now pay people to film chores. Chore data saturates quickly, so experts are the next scarce input. The skilled-trades retirement wave is peaking. Maintenance and diagnosis copilots need reasoning traces, not just video.
revenue_model: Employer capture fee of $6-15k per expert; dataset licensing at roughly $100-500 per hour of expert footage with recurring buyers; a follow-on 'build your maintenance copilot' project; royalty pass-through to experts as the trust mechanism.
non_obvious_insight: The highest-value physical-AI data is not being crowd-sourced. It sits in the heads and hands of people who were never recorded, and their employers will pay to capture it for their own continuity reasons. That makes the training data a subsidized by-product, undercutting gig-data vendors on cost and beating them on quality. Royalty-sharing with the expert defuses the consent and labor fight that will otherwise hit the data industry.
first_30_days: Choose one vertical, either municipal wastewater operators or CNC machinists. Recruit 5 soon-to-retire experts through state rural-water associations or machining trade newsletters. Run two paid pilots at a $2.5k intro price with a $400 camera kit. Cut a 20-hour sample reel and send it to 10 robotics and industrial-AI startups to collect letters of intent.

title: Pooled Buyer Mandates for Group Discounts
one_liner: Thousands of buyer agents sign standing purchase mandates ('I will pay up to $X if 200 others join') and vendors bid to fill the pooled demand.
customer: Startups and SMBs (10-200 employees) buying SaaS and business services (renewals, business insurance, telecom). Buyers pay a success fee and vendors pay for pre-committed demand.
problem: Small buyers lack bargaining power and time, and group purchasing organizations serve hospitals and enterprises, not the long tail. Vendors offer volume discounts against committed volume they cannot see. Agent payment standards now include signed intent mandates (Google's AP2, Mastercard's Verifiable Intent) that capture limits and constraints, and AP2 explicitly anticipates group scenarios, yet no product pools them.
solution: A mandate pool where each buyer or their agent signs an intent mandate with price ceiling, term and threshold. The exchange aggregates by category, shows vendors a live demand curve with reservation prices, and runs a sealed-bid reverse auction when the threshold is met. Purchases execute through each buyer's own payment mandate. First category: annual SaaS renewals, a Vendr for the long tail.
why_now: AP2 (September 2025), Verifiable Intent and UCP provide the first standard way to hold cryptographically signed, pre-authorized purchase intent. Agents now run procurement tasks, and vendors moving to agent meters want volume signals.
revenue_model: 5-10% of buyer savings or a 2-4% vendor fee on pooled transactions.
non_obvious_insight: A signed intent is a binding, machine-readable limit order for goods, so small buyers can pre-commit credibly without a human negotiating. That credibility is what makes group buying scale, like Kickstarter for procurement.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 startups from a founder community to pledge to 5 popular tools through a web form (protocol integration later). Bring the demand curve to 5 vendors and close one pooled deal to prove price.

title: Convert Legacy RPA Bots Using Their Own Logs
one_liner: Use years of bot execution logs as free ground-truth tests to convert brittle RPA bots into monitored agents at a fixed price per bot.
customer: Mid-market companies (500-10,000 employees) with 20-300 UiPath, Blue Prism or Power Automate bots in finance ops, claims and HR, plus RPA consultancies as a channel.
problem: Vendor and consultancy estimates put RPA upkeep at several times license cost, and UI changes break bots constantly. Leaders want agents but fear regression, and migration advice is generic ('retire the brittle ones first'). RPA vendors are pivoting to agentic pitches themselves, which increases pressure without giving a safe method.
solution: Ingest bot definitions and run logs, replay historical inputs to a candidate agent, and differentially test its outputs against the bot's recorded outputs. Cut over each bot when parity passes a threshold, keep the old bot in shadow for 30 days, monitor for drift, and price per bot converted plus a run-and-monitor fee.
why_now: Computer-use agents can operate UIs reliably enough to compete with scripted bots, and RPA vendors are moving to orchestration. Budgets are earmarked because maintenance costs are visible.
revenue_model: $2-$6k per bot conversion plus $200-$500/month per bot run and monitoring, with revenue share for consultancy partners.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part of migrating automations is knowing the new one is right. Legacy bots have already produced years of labeled input-output pairs for free, which turns migration into differential testing.
first_30_days: Find 10 mid-market RPA shops and ask each for 5 brittle bots. Convert 5 bots across 2 customers in shadow mode, show parity, and sign a fixed-fee conversion for the next 20.

title: GLP-1 Palate Panel for Food R&D
one_liner: A managed panel of GLP-1 users and their households that food and restaurant companies rent to test products, portions and health claims.
customer: R&D and insights teams at mid-size CPG (protein, snacks, frozen), restaurant chain menu teams, foodservice for hospitals and senior living, and supplement brands that need claim substantiation ($25-150k per study).
problem: 73% of GLP-1 users report taste changes and 70% lose joy in eating, so 'just add protein' fails. About 70% change what the household eats, and non-users adopt 30-50% of the changes, so the affected base is ~50% larger than the user count. Food companies are reformulating and launching 'GLP-1 friendly' labels on general-population panels and conflicting forecasts.
solution: Recruit and maintain a segmented panel (drug, dose, weeks on therapy, aversion profile, household makeup). Run sensory, portion and format tests plus home-use tests and 8-12 week muscle and satiety claim studies. Deliver 'aversion maps' (which textures and smells trigger nausea at which dose) and household spillover models.
why_now: Households with a GLP-1 user doubled from ~11% to 22% in under 3 years. Pills launched in 2026 broaden the base. CPG is mid-reformulation, and FTC claim scrutiny makes 'evidence-backed' labels valuable. Purchase-panel incumbents see what is bought, not why.
revenue_model: $25-150k per study, plus $40-100k/year data subscription for 'aversion map' updates.
non_obvious_insight: The 'GLP-1 consumer' is 5-6 sensory segments that shift with dose and week on therapy, not one persona. Forecasting from sales data cannot separate them, but a panel can. The picks-and-shovels of a reformulation wave are the testers, not the brands.
first_30_days: Recruit 300 panelists from subreddits and Facebook groups with a $25 incentive, verified by photo of the pharmacy label. Publish a free 'taste change' survey report for press. Cold-email 30 CPG insights leads and land a first paid pilot of about $25k.

title: Hybrid-Race-in-a-Box Rentals for Gyms
one_liner: Rentable station kits, timing, waivers, insurance and sanitation protocols so any gym can run a Hyrox-style event for members.
customer: Independent gyms and CrossFit-style boxes (pay $2.5-4k per event); secondary: run-club organizers and corporate wellness days.
problem: Chain: Hyrox's global boom (events selling out, new markets such as Kuala Lumpur in December 2026) makes members demand local competitions, but official events are capacity-limited and licensed; local copycats need eight stations of gear, timing, heat management and a medical plan; and the Beijing incident (an athlete kept racing after soiling herself on shared equipment, prompting an apology and new biohazard rules) shows sanitation is a brand-level risk. Nobody sells a standardized, insured kit.
solution: A trailerized 8-station kit with standard loading specs, chip or QR bib timing through a phone app, wipe-down protocol cards and biohazard kit, medical response plan, waiver and event-insurance pack, and a results page. The gym sells tickets; we take rental plus a per-athlete fee.
why_now: Hybrid racing went mainstream in 2025-26, hygiene and safety incidents have made organizers seek documented protocols, and used sleds and ergs are cheap.
revenue_model: $2.5-4k per event rental plus about $5 per athlete for timing and insurance; sell kits to multi-gym operators at $18-30k.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not the format but the logistics and liability packaging for local operators; for a gym the payoff is member retention and lead generation from ticket buyers who are not yet members.
first_30_days: Buy $12-15k of used sleds, ballast and ergs, run a first event with a partner gym to document cost per athlete, offer three other gyms discounted rentals, and build a small QR-bib timing page.

title: After-School Shop Clubs Run by Retired Tradespeople
one_liner: Screen-free after-school care for ages 10-15 inside idle trade-school and union shops, staffed by retired journeymen who teach kids to build real things.
customer: Parents of 10-15-year-olds paying about $180-260 a month, plus sponsors (contractor associations, distributors, JATCs and local subs) paying $150-300 per enrolled kid as a recruiting pipeline. State child-care subsidy vouchers where the program is licensed.
problem: School-age care from 3 to 6pm is scarce, and Gen Alpha teens fill it with phones and AI companions (72% of US teens have used them) while under-16 social bans leak. Most of the trades labor gap is retirements, and the pipeline is thinner than headlines suggest (the enrollment surge is called a demographic mirage). Community-college and JATC shops sit empty after 3pm. Retired tradespeople lose purpose and have no channel to pass on skills.
solution: Run a licensed or license-exempt (per state rule) after-school program in partner shops. One certified childcare lead plus paid retired journeyman mentors ($25-30/hr from sponsor funds) run projects such as tiny houses, cabinetry, wiring boards and plumbing trees. Phones stay in lockers. Older kids earn micro-credentials (OSHA-10 at 16, NCCER Core) and sponsors get first look. A small local team can run in three shops in year one.
why_now: Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia have under-16 bans, US school phone bans cover 12 states, and parents want credible offline options. ROAD to Housing Act standard plans and manufactured-home reforms are creating build content and demand for skilled set crews. The retirement wave is driving most of the ABC 349K and 456K worker gap.
revenue_model: Tuition $180-260 per child per month, sponsor fees $150-300 per child per month (or lump-sum program sponsorship), subsidy vouchers where eligible, and mentor stipends funded through sponsorship.
non_obvious_insight: The apprenticeship pipeline's real bottleneck is exposure and mentors before age 16, not training seats. Idle shops, retired mentors and parents desperate for screen-free care are three underused assets that pay for each other. A contractor who pays $3K to keep a local kid in the trades over two years is spending less than the cost of one bad hire.
first_30_days: Partner with one community college, ABC or IEC chapter training center. Recruit three retired journeymen and confirm the state licensing exemption (or license a school-age program). Run an 8-week pilot three afternoons a week for 12 kids at $180 a month, with $500 sponsorships from five local subs, and fill the waitlist through local parent Facebook groups.

title: Independent Lab Certifying AI Detectors and Watermarks
one_liner: An AV-TEST-style lab that red-teams detectors and watermarks every month and sells certification seals and buyer reports.
customer: Detection and watermark vendors (seals and re-tests), and enterprise buyers such as platform trust-and-safety teams, publishers, insurers and law firms that need to know which tool to trust.
problem: Detection is crowded and cheap (Pangram $9M raise at $20/month, GPTZero $10M, GetReal $18M, Reality Defender $15M, Deezer licensing its detector) and buyers cannot verify accuracy claims. Pangram claims about 1 in 10,000 false positives, yet a reviewer still saw human sentences flagged. Watermark removers appeared within a week of Sora. Public 'human vs AI' scores now shape reputations, but no one audits them.
solution: A monthly adversarial benchmark across text, audio, image and video. It uses stratified known-human gold sets (for example non-native English writers and niche music genres), fresh output from current models, adaptive attacks (paraphrasers, re-encoding, watermark removers) and fixed false-positive operating points. Publish a leaderboard, and issue 'certified at or below X% false-positive rate on domain Y' seals and watermark robustness ratings.
why_now: Detectors are being embedded in reader-facing features (Substack, LinkedIn, Deezer licensing), EU Art. 50 pushes marking and detection into procurement checklists, and reputational stakes for false positives are visible.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per vendor for testing and seals, $5-25k/year buyer subscriptions for detailed results, and $10-40k custom bake-offs.
non_obvious_insight: When the buyer cannot verify a product's core claim, the independent tester captures value, which is why UL, AV-TEST and NSS Labs exist. The scarce asset is a fresh, curated, known-human gold set plus an adversarial toolkit.
first_30_days: Publish a free benchmark v0 of six text detectors and three audio detectors in three weeks, using 2,000 volunteer-written human documents and fresh AI outputs. DM vendors and trust-and-safety leads with a paid 'verified retest' offer. First payers will be challengers who want a credible badge.

title: Dr. Simi USA: Pharmacy-Plus-Consult for the Uninsured
one_liner: Small-format, generic-first pharmacies with a nurse-practitioner consult room beside the counter, posted cash prices and no insurance needed, following Mexico's Farmacias Similares model and landing in US pharmacy deserts.
customer: Uninsured and underinsured adults in pharmacy deserts and immigrant neighborhoods. An estimated 4.8M Americans lost coverage after the enhanced ACA subsidies expired, and about 48M people live in pharmacy deserts. The second customer is at-risk independent pharmacists who license the clinic kit.
problem: Rite Aid is gone (all stores closed after its 2025 Chapter 11), Walgreens is shrinking, and independents are squeezed by PBM reimbursement. An uninsured person with a UTI or sinus infection faces a $150-250 urgent-care visit plus retail drug prices, so many just skip treatment.
solution: An 800-1,200 sq ft store or a 200 sq ft conversion inside an existing independent pharmacy. A flat $25-40 NP consult (loss leader), point-of-care tests (strep, flu, UTI, A1c), on-site dispensing of generics at transparent cost-plus prices, bilingual staff, and chronic-refill programs. The visit and the dispense happen in one 10-minute stop, so there is no abandoned prescription. Mexico's Farmacias Similares runs thousands of outlets with an attached doctor's office charging a few dollars.
why_now: Coverage is shrinking at the same time as pharmacy access: enhanced ACA subsidies lapsed at the end of 2025, Medicaid cuts phase in through 2026-27, and Rite Aid's liquidation left holes in low-income neighborhoods. Cost Plus Drugs has taught Americans to expect transparent generic prices, so a cash-price store is no longer strange.
revenue_model: Dispensing margin on generics, flat consult fees, point-of-care lab fees, OTC sales, plus licensing or franchise fees for the turnkey clinic-in-a-pharmacy kit sold to independents.
non_obvious_insight: Don't compete with telehealth on convenience; win on adjacency. Consult plus dispense in one stop removes the biggest leak in cash-pay care, which is people who get a prescription and never fill it. The fastest route isn't building stores at all. It is converting existing independents on the edge of closure by giving them a second revenue line, and an already-licensed pharmacy removes months of setup.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 independent pharmacies in Latino neighborhoods (Texas, Florida or Illinois). Contract per-diem NPs under a collaborative practice agreement, build a 100 sq ft consult room, and print a simple price list ('$29 visit, $4 generics'). Market through WhatsApp groups, churches and community radio. Run a 60-day pilot and track visit-to-fill conversion and margin per visit.

title: Post-Divorce Beneficiary Cleanup for Family Lawyers
one_liner: Sell divorce attorneys a flat-fee sweep that finds and fixes stale beneficiary designations, since the will is the least important estate document.
customer: Family-law attorneys and divorce mediators or CDFAs. The initial buyer is the law firm, which adds it to the closing checklist. It expands later to advisors and benefits platforms.
problem: Most middle-class wealth passes by beneficiary designation (401(k)s, IRAs, life insurance, TOD/POD accounts), not by will. For ERISA plans the plan documents generally control even when the divorce decree says otherwise (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, Kennedy v. Plan Administrator). Clients rarely update every form. Ex-spouses get paid, second families litigate, and the lawyer faces malpractice exposure.
solution: A 'Post-Decree Beneficiary Sweep'. The client links accounts or uploads statements. Software plus a paralegal gets each custodian's current designation, compares it to the decree, will and trust, and produces a discrepancy report. It prepares custodian-specific change forms for e-signature and tracks each until confirmed. A yearly re-audit subscription follows, triggered by life events (birth, remarriage, death).
why_now: Account aggregation and LLM extraction from messy statements and custodian PDFs now make cross-custodian paperwork cheap. Retirement balances sit at record levels, and divorce among the over-50s ('grey divorce') has risen for decades. The transfer wave is putting designation errors in the spotlight.
revenue_model: $295-$495 flat per divorce billed as a firm disbursement, $79/yr monitoring, and an enterprise license to benefits platforms and advisors at roughly $1-3 per participant per year.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in estate planning talks about wills and trusts. The biggest mis-transfers happen through forms nobody re-reads. Divorce is the one moment when a lawyer, a deadline and malpractice fear are all in the room, so it is the cheapest place to sell an audit.
first_30_days: Sell to 10 solo and small family-law firms as a flat add-on. Process the first 20 cases manually with a paralegal and spreadsheet. Track the share of clients whose ex-spouse is still named anywhere (a hypothesis to measure) and turn that into a case study and a malpractice-avoidance pitch.
